opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core thing the time horizon metric gives you is a unit that's actually interpretable and that doesn't saturate the way benchmarks usually do. With most benchmarks, you get a percentage score, say 60% on some dataset, and it's really hard to know what that means in the real world. And then a year or two later the benchmark is at 95% and you have to build a new one, and you can't easily compare scores across them. So you end up with this patchwork of numbers that don't connect to each other.

What we tried to do with time horizon is anchor the difficulty of tasks to something concrete: how long it takes a skilled human professional, someone with the relevant expertise, to complete the task. Then for a given model, we ask roughly: at what human task length does this model succeed about 50% of the time? That gives you a number in minutes or hours, and minutes and hours mean something to people. If a model has a one-hour time horizon on software tasks, you have some intuition for what kinds of work that might cover, and also what it doesn't cover yet.

The other big thing is that it lets you put models from very different eras on the same axis. We could measure GPT-2-era models, which basically can't do anything beyond a few seconds of work, all the way up to current frontier models, on one scale. When you do that, you see a surprisingly clean trend. Time horizon has been doubling roughly every seven months over the past several years, and maybe faster more recently. That kind of long-run, consistent trend is really useful if you care about forecasting, because you can at least ask, "If this continues, when do we get to models that can do day-long or week-long or month-long projects autonomously?" Those are the thresholds that matter a lot for thinking about economic impact and risk.

I want to be careful not to oversell it, though. There are a lot of caveats. Our task suites are mostly software engineering and research-flavored tasks, they're relatively well-specified, they have automatic scoring, and they're often less "messy" than real-world work. So the specific numbers shouldn't be read as "models can now do any one-hour job." And the 50% threshold is a choice; if you look at 80% reliability, the horizons are quite a bit shorter. But as a way of tracking the trend in autonomous capability over time in a unit people can reason about, I think it's filled a gap that standard benchmarks weren't really filling.

r001.rationale: The response discusses benchmark saturation, human task duration, and model reliability, but does not say that AI can succeed on exceptionally difficult problems while failing at ordinary practical tasks.

r002.rationale: It anchors task difficulty to how long a skilled professional takes, then uses the model’s success at those task lengths to track autonomous capability. The response presents this as an approximate measure and notes caveats.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that's distinctive about time horizon is that it's trying to put model capabilities on a scale that's actually meaningful outside of the benchmark itself. Most benchmarks give you a number between zero and a hundred, and that number is only interpretable relative to other models on that same benchmark. If I tell you a model gets 60 percent on some agentic coding eval, you have no idea what that means unless you already know what the tasks are, how hard they are, how long they take people to do. And the scores saturate, so every couple years you have to make a new one, and now you've lost comparability with the old one.

Time horizon tries to fix that by anchoring to something external, which is how long it takes a human expert to do the task. So instead of saying "the model gets 60 percent," you say "the model can reliably do tasks that take a skilled human about an hour." That's a unit that doesn't go stale. An hour means the same thing in 2023 as it does in 2026, so you can actually put models from different years on the same axis and ask how fast the frontier is moving. And it turned out, when we did that, that the trend was surprisingly regular, something like doubling every seven months or so over the past several years, which is a much more useful thing to know than any individual benchmark score.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that it gives you a handle on the question people actually care about, which is something like, what fraction of real work can these systems do? Human labor is pretty naturally decomposed into tasks of different lengths, and a lot of the economically important stuff is long. So if you know the horizon is at an hour and it's doubling every seven months, you can start to reason about when it hits a day, or a week, and what that would mean. You can't really do that kind of extrapolation with a saturating benchmark.

I should say there are real limitations. The tasks we use are much cleaner than real-world work: they're well specified, they have automatic scoring, there's no messy context or ambiguous goals. So the absolute numbers are probably optimistic, and the fifty-percent-success threshold we usually quote is a pretty low bar for actually relying on a system. But I think the trend is the robust part, and the fact that it's expressed in a unit people can intuitively reason about is the main thing the metric buys you.

r001.rationale: The response discusses benchmark limitations and imperfect real-world tasks, but does not say that systems can succeed at exceptionally difficult human problems while failing at ordinary practical tasks.

r002.rationale: It describes using the time a skilled human takes to complete a task as the external scale for model capability, presenting human task duration as a proxy for the task’s demands.

astra-6.text:
I think the distinctive value is that it gives us a way to talk about capabilities in terms of the length of tasks that an AI can complete, rather than just its score on a particular benchmark. Roughly, you take tasks, measure how long they take a human, and ask how reliably the model can complete tasks of that duration. So a 50 percent time horizon of an hour means that, on the task distribution you’re evaluating, the model succeeds about half the time on tasks that take a human an hour.

That’s useful because a benchmark score can be pretty hard to interpret. If a model goes from 40 percent to 60 percent, how much more useful is it? How much closer is it to doing a substantial project autonomously? Time horizon gives us a somewhat more intuitive scale, and potentially one that we can keep using as models improve.

The caveat is that human completion time doesn’t capture everything that makes a task hard for an AI, and the task distribution matters a lot. An hour-long coding task and an hour-long conversation aren’t interchangeable. So I’d view it as a useful measure of how long models can sustain successful work in the domains we test, rather than a universal measure of intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts benchmark scores with completing substantial projects, but does not say that AI can succeed on exceptionally difficult problems while failing at ordinary practical tasks.

r002.rationale: It describes human task duration as a way to measure the length of tasks, but does not present that duration as a tentative proxy for the agency needed to complete them or specify humans with suitable expertise.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the distinctive value is that it puts capabilities in units that are meaningful to people. If I tell you a model gets a certain score on a benchmark, it’s often hard to translate that into what you could actually use it for. If I tell you it can reliably complete tasks that take a human an hour, that gives you a more concrete sense of what you might delegate to it.

It also gets at something that short questions can miss, which is whether a model can sustain useful work over a longer sequence of steps. Being able to do each individual step reasonably well doesn’t necessarily mean you can complete the whole task reliably.

There are caveats, though. A task taking a human a long time doesn’t uniquely specify how difficult it is for an AI, and the kinds of tasks you sample matter a lot. So I’d view time horizon as a useful, interpretable summary of a particular set of capabilities, rather than a complete measure of intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response discusses benchmark scores and tasks that take humans an hour, but does not say AI can succeed at exceptionally difficult problems while failing at ordinary practical tasks.

r002.rationale: The response uses human task duration as an interpretable indicator of what could be delegated, but does not specify humans with suitable expertise or frame task duration as a proxy for the agency required.
